title: Show Your Sources

post.author: u/night_steno_clowance
post.title: Our agency's assistant quoted a witness from my own transcript, with a page and a line number. I was in the room. She never said it.

blocks.text: I'm a court stenographer. By day I take depositions for Polglase Verbatim, a small reporting agency; at night I edit the transcripts at my kitchen table, page by page, line by line. Since the spring the agency has had an assistant: a lawyer types a question about a transcript, and it answers with a quotation and its page and line. About 160 questions a night.

It reads our transcripts in pieces. The script that loads them cuts each one every 240 characters, keeps the page and line numbers to look up, and drops the column with the speakers' names. The system prompt says to answer from the transcript and quote it exactly. The temperature is 0.7. On Tuesday night, a solicitor asked about one of mine.

23:12  solicitor  Did the witness see the car before nine?
23:12  assistant  Yes. The witness said, "I saw the blue car at ten to
                   nine" (p. 41, l. 12).

I took that deposition. Mrs Tresidder was in the bakery on Bossiney Row the morning a cyclist was knocked down outside. I opened page 41. At line 12 she says: I never saw a car at ten to nine. Two lines down, at line 14, Mr Carveth, the driver's barrister, reads her the driver's statement: I saw the blue car at the corner.
The line had a page, a line number and an oath behind it. Nobody in that room ever said it.

On Saturday I asked the assistant eight questions about page 41 whose answers I know by heart. Two of them have no answer on the page; it answered both anyway. Of the eight quotations it gave me, three were Mrs Tresidder's own words at the line it named. Then I printed the piece it had read for the car question and drew it.

blocks.label: page41_piece2.png

diagram.aria: Clowance's drawing of the piece the assistant read. Left, two lines of page 41: line 12, Mrs Tresidder, the witness: I never saw a car at ten to nine. Line 14, Mr Carveth, reading the driver's statement: I saw the blue car at the corner. Both run into piece 2 of 3, characters 240 to 479, with no speaker names. From the piece, the answer at 23:12 on Tuesday: I saw the blue car at ten to nine, cited at page 41, line 12. Nobody on page 41 said these words.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing haunts page 41; the assistant wrote that line. What you want from it is grounding: every answer resting only on the text it was handed. A speaker turn is one person's stretch of talk, from their name to the next name. A claim is one thing an answer asserts, here each quotation with its page and line. Faithfulness is the share of claims the source supports: supported claims divided by all claims, measured over a set of questions. You've measured it already. Three questions. When it gave p. 41, l. 12, did it copy those words out of the transcript, or write them and then look up a line? Could anything in piece 2 tell Mrs Tresidder from Mr Carveth? And on your two questions with no answer on the page, what was it allowed to say?

replies.author: u/night_steno_clowance
replies.text: It writes the quotations itself; citations are off. The provider's docs list three kinds of document for citations: plain text, PDF, and custom content, which is a list of blocks you cut yourself, each one citable. We send each piece as plain text, and piece 2 has no names in it, only words. The prompt says nothing about answers that aren't there, so asked the colour of the cyclist's coat, it said yellow. There's no coat on page 41.

comments.author: u/zero_temp_gwinear
comments.text: Your problem is the 0.7. Temperature is randomness: above zero it samples, and sampling is where invented text comes from. At 0 it takes the likeliest word every time, so it can only say what the transcript makes most likely, and you get the same answer on every run, which is what a court wants. I build tools for law firms and every one of them runs at zero. Set it, rerun your eight, done.

replies.author: u/gradient_ghost
replies.text: Worth a try before Monday. If it runs at 0 and gives the same answer every time, which answer will it give to the car question?

comments.author: u/nankervis_for_claimant
comments.text: I'm the solicitor who asked. I act for the cyclist. At 23:14 I pasted that line into a draft letter to the driver's insurers, with its page and line, because it had a page and line. I stopped only because I wanted the exact wording and opened page 41 myself. It isn't there. I've read that page four times since, and every time I half expect to find it.

replies.author: u/night_steno_clowance
replies.text: Thank you for opening the page. I'll send you a certified copy of 41 in the morning.

reply.prompt: The agency wants the assistant back on Monday night. What should Clowance change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Give each speaker turn its own cited block, check every quote against the page, and allow not found.
options.part2: On Sunday I rebuilt the loader: one block per speaker turn, each starting with the speaker's name and keeping its page and line, sent as a custom content document with citations on. Every quotation in the answer's own words is string-matched against the block it cites, and the prompt allows not found. Monday, 23:40, the same solicitor asked the same question. No. The witness said, "I never saw a car at ten to nine" (p. 41, l. 12), and under it Mrs Tresidder's whole turn, copied from the transcript with her name. On my eight questions: 6 of 6 claims supported. The check struck two quotations it wrote in its own prose, "It was raining" for a witness who said I think it might have been raining, and "by the church clock", which she never said. Asked the colour of the cyclist's coat, it said not found. As a test I put the pieces back to 240 characters with everything else on, and the driver question came back as hers: 6 of 7.
options.senior: Make the source do the quoting. One block per speaker turn means a cited span is always whole turns with their speakers' names, never a fragment pieced from inside two; citations copy the cited text from the source, so it can't drift. The quote check catches what the model still writes in its own prose, and not found gives it an honest way out. Then measure faithfulness on a fixed set, and count what it leaves unanswered too.

options.text: Add a firm line to the system prompt: never invent, alter or join quotations, and quote the page exactly.
options.part2: I added the line in capitals. On Saturday's eight questions the assistant gave the same answers, word for word: "I saw the blue car at ten to nine" (p. 41, l. 12), "It was raining", the yellow coat. Faithfulness 3 of 8, as before. It wasn't disobeying. Piece 2 holds both phrases and no names, and it believed every quotation it wrote was on the page. The next Tuesday night a lawyer asked whether Mrs Tresidder had seen the driver, and it said yes, with Mr Carveth's line 14.
options.senior: A prompt line asks; it can't check, and it can't give the model what the chunk threw away. The model had no speaker names and wrote its quotations from memory of the chunk, so it couldn't tell an invented quote from a real one. Fix what it reads and what it copies, then check the result in code.

options.text: Set the temperature to 0, so the assistant gives the same careful answer to each question every time.
options.part2: Temperature 0. I asked the car question five times in a row. Five times: Yes. The witness said, "I saw the blue car at ten to nine" (p. 41, l. 12). Only the wording of the lead-in had ever changed at 0.7, never the quotation. On the eight questions, 3 of 8 again. It is now very reliable about a sentence nobody said.
options.senior: Temperature changes how the next word is drawn, not what the model was given. A stitched quote from a nameless chunk is often the likeliest text, so at 0 you get it every time. Anthropic's API reference says even temperature 0 is not fully deterministic, and its newer models reject any value but 1.0. Repeatable is not the same as faithful.

options.text: Have a stenographer read each answer against the transcript, line by line, before it reaches a lawyer.
options.verdict: Trade-off: faithful, at a night's work
options.part2: I read every answer against the transcript before it went out. At three minutes each, 160 answers is 8 hours, my whole night; the editing waited. On the eight-question set I struck 5 claims and sent 3, all supported, 3 of 3. But three questions the page does answer went back with nothing, the car, the rain and the time of the bang, because every quotation in them was wrong and I had no time to write the answers myself. The lawyers got them in the morning.
options.senior: A person checking everything is faithful and doesn't scale: the cost grows with every question, and the model keeps inventing, you just catch it. Use people to check a sample and to build the question set. Let the system copy its quotations from the source and check them in code.

sim.title: Rerun page 41 yourself
sim.lede: You're Clowance on Saturday, rerunning page 41. There is no real model. The sim holds page 41 of Mrs Tresidder's deposition as twelve speaker turns, lines 2 to 24: each turn takes two lines, the speaker's name and then the words, and is cited by its first line. Mr Carveth asks on lines 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22; she answers on lines 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24. It holds your eight questions, six that page 41 answers and two it doesn't, and a stand-in that follows stated rules in place of a model. Chunking: either the words of all twelve turns joined without names, 631 characters cut every 240 into 3 pieces, or one block per speaker turn, each starting with the speaker's name. Without citations the stand-in writes each quotation itself, and gives the line where the last words it used appear. In one piece it joins two phrases that answer a question, and it rewrites two quotations from memory: Q2's hedge goes, and Q3 gains words. With citations on, its quotation is the cited text, copied from the source: the sentence holding it (plain-text pieces are cited by sentence) or the whole block; its prose may still carry its own version as a second claim. With no answer on the page, in nameless pieces it takes Mr Carveth's line 14 for the witness's on the driver question; otherwise it says not found if allowed, or guesses. A claim is supported if the quoted words are Mrs Tresidder's own at the line given. The quote check is a string match: in pieces it can only confirm the words occur somewhere on the page; in blocks it confirms them in the cited block, and that the block is hers. The hand check strikes every unsupported claim: 160 answers a night at 3 minutes each. Temperature changes only the opening words, and the prompt line changes nothing the stand-in can see.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the night: 240-character pieces, nothing else on, temperature 0.7. Q1 says "I saw the blue car at ten to nine" (p. 41, l. 12), and faithfulness on the set is 3 of 8. Set the temperature to 0: one wording in 5 reruns, the same quote, 3 of 8. Add the prompt line: 3 of 8. Switch to one block per speaker turn: Q1 now quotes line 12 as spoken, 4 of 8. Turn citations on: 6 of 10. Add the quote check: 6 of 6, with 4 quotations struck and two questions sent nothing. Allow not found: 6 of 6, not found 2 of 2. Now switch back to 240-character pieces with all that on, and pick Q7: it gives Mr Carveth's line 14 as hers, 6 of 7. Back to the night, try the quote check alone (3 of 4, three real answers lost) and the hand check (3 of 3, 8 h 0 min a night).

explain.oneLine: Nothing rewrote page 41. The assistant read a piece of transcript with no speaker names, wrote its quotation from memory of it, and joined line 14's words to line 12's. Copy quotations from blocks that keep the speaker, check them, and let it say not found.

steps.title: The pieces had no speakers.
steps.text: The loader cut page 41 every 240 characters and dropped the names. Piece 2 held the end of Mrs Tresidder's answer and all of Mr Carveth's question as one run of words, so nothing in it said that "I saw the blue car" was the driver's statement read aloud, not the witness. This is a3e02's lesson about metadata from the other side: a chunk needs to carry who said it, not just where it sits.

steps.title: It quoted from memory.
steps.text: With citations off, the model writes its quotations itself, like any other text, and then attaches a page and line. Text it writes can drift from the source: Q2 lost its hedge, "I think it might have been raining" became "It was raining", and Q1 joined two phrases from one piece into a sentence nobody spoke. Asking it in the prompt not to invent quotes doesn't help when it can't tell an invented quote from a real one.

steps.title: Citations copy the words, and blocks keep the speaker.
steps.text: Anthropic's citations feature returns each claim with the source text that supports it, and the API copies that cited text from your document rather than the model writing it. Plain text and PDFs are cut into sentences; a custom content document uses your own blocks as they are, and a citation names a range of whole blocks. Make each speaker turn one block, starting with the speaker's name, and a cited span is always whole turns with their names on them, never a fragment from inside two.

steps.title: Check every quotation, and allow not found.
steps.text: The model can still put its own words in quotation marks in its prose, outside the cited span. So check every quotation in the answer by string match against the block it cites, and that the block belongs to the speaker it names; strike what fails. When the transcript doesn't answer, "not found" must be an allowed answer, or the model guesses: the yellow coat. Count an honest not found as a good answer, not a failure.

steps.title: Measure faithfulness on a set.
steps.text: Faithfulness is supported claims divided by all claims, over a fixed set of questions with known answers, some of which the documents can't answer. Clowance's eight questions went from 3 of 8 to 6 of 6. Count answerable questions left unanswered beside it, because an assistant that says not found to everything makes no claims and can't score badly.

diagram.aria: The fix for Monday. Left, two of page 41's twelve blocks, one per speaker turn: block 5, Mrs Tresidder, the witness, page 41 line 12, I never saw a car at ten to nine; block 6, Mr Carveth, counsel, line 14, the driver's statement read aloud. Both feed the quote check in the middle, a string match in the cited block. Right, two answers: Q1, No, she never saw it, cited block 5, page 41 line 12; Q6, the colour of the coat, not found, because no block holds it.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Monday night. Each speaker turn is its own block, starting with the speaker's name and keeping its page and line. The answer to Q1 cites block 5, Mrs Tresidder's whole turn at line 12, and the quote check confirms its quotation is in that block and that the block is hers. Mr Carveth's block 6 can be cited, but never as the witness. Q6 has no block to cite, so the answer is not found.

fix.title: The fix: one cited block per speaker turn, a quote check, and not found
fix.text: Load each transcript as one block per speaker turn, with the speaker's name at the start of the block and its page and line kept with it, and send the blocks as a custom content document with citations on. Show lawyers the cited text under each answer. Check every quotation in the answer's prose by string match against the block it cites, and that the block's speaker is the one the answer names; strike what fails. Allow "not found", and say so in the prompt. Before each change, run a fixed question set with known answers and record faithfulness and the answerable questions left unanswered.

limits: Citations show where a claim came from, not that the claim follows from it. A cited block can be quoted faithfully and still be read wrongly, such as a hedge treated as a yes, so faithfulness still needs measuring on a set.
A string match only catches quotations. A claim the model puts in its own words, with no quotation marks, passes the check, so judging those still needs a person or a second model on a sample.
Citations can't be combined with structured outputs on Anthropic's API, which returns an error, so an assistant that must reply in a fixed JSON shape needs another way to carry its sources.

explain.seniorTake: Grounding fails quietly when the model writes the evidence itself. Decide what the source must carry, here who spoke and where, and make it the unit you cite, so the system copies quotations instead of composing them. Then check every quotation in code, give the model an honest way to say the answer isn't there, and measure faithfulness on a fixed set, with the answers it failed to give counted beside it.

realWorld.title: Anthropic citations: three document types, read 11 October 2026
realWorld.text: Anthropic's citations documentation lists plain text, chunked by sentence and cited by character index; PDF, chunked by sentence and cited by page number; and custom content, best for lists and transcripts, with no additional chunking and cited by block index. It adds: if you need more control over citation granularity (for example, for bullet points or transcripts), use custom content documents instead.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: cited text is copied, not written
realWorld.text: The same page says that because the API parses citations and extracts cited_text directly, citations are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents, and that cited_text does not count toward output tokens.

realWorld.title: Anthropic API reference: whole blocks only
realWorld.text: For a custom content document the citation type is content_block_location. Its cited_text always equals the contents of content[start_block_index:end_block_index] joined together, and the reference says the text block is the minimal citable unit; this field is never a substring of a single block.

realWorld.title: Anthropic API reference: temperature
realWorld.text: The reference says that even with temperature of 0.0, the results will not be fully deterministic, and marks temperature deprecated: models released after Claude Opus 4.6 accept only 1.0 and reject other values with a 400 error.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: allow I don't know, verify with citations
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations suggests explicitly giving Claude permission to admit uncertainty, and having it find a supporting quote for each claim after it answers: if it can't find a quote, it must retract the claim.

realWorld.title: Cohere: fine-grained citations
realWorld.text: Cohere's documentation says its Chat endpoint generates fine-grained citations for its RAG response, each with the start and end indices of the text that cites a source and the source or sources it references. As with any citation, a check of the quoted words is still yours to add.

realWorld.title: Ragas, 2023: faithfulness as a fraction
realWorld.text: Es and colleagues say an answer is faithful to its context if the claims that are made in the answer can be inferred from the context, and score it as F = |V|/|S|: the number of statements that were supported over the total number of statements.

asked: How do you stop a RAG system from making things up?
interview.answer: First, ground it: send the retrieved text with the question, tell it to answer only from that, and allow an explicit not found, because a model with no permission to say so will guess. For citations I'd make the cited unit match what the reader must trust: for a transcript, one block per speaker turn with the name and page and line kept, sent as custom content with citations on, so the cited text is copied from the source and can't drift. Then a code check on every quotation in the prose against the block it cites, striking what fails. To measure, I keep a fixed set of questions with known answers, including some the documents can't answer, split answers into claims and report supported claims over all claims, with answerable questions left unanswered beside it, and rerun it before every change. Temperature doesn't come into it: repeatable is not faithful.

terms.def: A person who records everything said in a hearing or deposition, word for word, and produces the official transcript. Clowance takes depositions by day and edits at night.
A firm that sends stenographers to depositions and hearings and sells the transcripts to lawyers. Polglase Verbatim is a small one.
A witness's sworn evidence, given before a trial in answer to lawyers' questions and taken down word for word.
The written record of what was said, numbered by page and line so lawyers can point to any line exactly.
How lawyers cite a transcript: page 41, line 12. On page 41 each turn takes two lines, the speaker's name and the words, and is cited by its first line.
In England and Wales, a lawyer who advises a client and runs their case. This one acts for the cyclist.
In England and Wales, a lawyer who argues cases and questions witnesses. Mr Carveth acts for the driver.
The lawyer asking the questions, here Mr Carveth.
A written account a witness signs before trial. Mr Carveth reads from the driver's statement on line 14.
The company that would pay for the driver if the driver were found at fault.
A copy of a transcript page signed by the stenographer as a true copy of the record.
One person's stretch of talk, from their name to the next name. Page 41 has twelve.
One thing an answer asserts. Here each quotation with its page and line is one claim.
A claim the source backs. In the sim: the quoted words are the witness's own, at the line the answer gives.
The share of an answer's claims the source supports: supported claims divided by all claims, measured over a set of questions.
A fixed list of questions with known answers, some the documents can't answer, run before every change. Clowance's has eight.
Clowance's word for one 240-character chunk of the transcript, cut with no regard for speakers. Page 41 makes 3.
A quotation joined from words in two places, here two speakers, so it reads as one sentence that nobody said.
A quotation the model rewrote while writing it out: a hedge dropped, a word added. Q2 and Q3 in the sim.
Words that make a statement less certain, such as I think or might have been.
An API feature: switch it on for a document and each claim in the reply comes with the source text that supports it and where it is.
The exact source text behind a citation, which the API copies from your document rather than the model writing it.
A document sent as one string. For citations it is cut into sentences and cited by character position.
A document sent as a list of blocks you cut yourself. For citations no further cutting is done, and a citation names a range of whole blocks.
One item in a custom content document's list, the smallest unit it can cite. On Monday, one speaker turn.
A block's place in the list, counted from 0. A citation gives a start index and an end index that is not included.
The citation type returned for custom content documents: the cited text, the document and the block index range.
Code that tests each quotation in an answer by string match against the source it cites, and strikes it if absent.
Testing whether one piece of text appears exactly, character for character, inside another.
An allowed answer saying the documents don't hold what was asked. An honest not found counts as a good answer.
Remove a claim from an answer before it is sent.
A person reading every answer against the source before it goes out. In the sim, 3 minutes an answer.
The sim's fixed rules that play the model's part, so every run gives the same answers and the lesson can be checked.
A company that offers language models through an API, including chat with citations for RAG.
Cohere's term for citations that each point a span of the answer, by start and end index, at the sources it rests on.
A 2023 paper and toolkit for scoring RAG answers automatically, including faithfulness. LATENT Season 5 returns to it.
What Ragas calls a claim: one short assertion split out of an answer, checked against the context.
An assistant that answers questions about a company's contracts from the contract documents.
A contract goes through drafts before one version is signed. Only the signed one binds the parties.
One numbered section of a contract.
Where an assistant's source documents are kept and searched.
A screen of live numbers about a system, such as a weekly faithfulness score.
The output criterion in the processing integrity category of the 2017 Trust Services Criteria: outputs delivered completely and accurately.
The street with the bakery where Mrs Tresidder stood, in the story.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that quotes documents to people who act on the quote: a contracts assistant, a policy bot, a support assistant that cites help articles. A common incident: a contracts assistant quotes a clause, with its number, that was in a draft, not the signed version, because both versions sat in the document store as plain text with nothing to tell them apart. Ask three things. Does each chunk carry what the reader must trust, such as which version, which section, who said it? Are quotations copied from the source by a citations feature, or written by the model? Is every quotation checked in code against the text it cites? The usual fix is citations to the signed document's blocks, with the version kept on each block, and a quote check that strikes any quotation not found in the block it cites. Keep a question set with known answers, including questions the documents can't answer, and record faithfulness and the answerable questions left unanswered before each change. Standards-readiness note: if your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes the processing integrity category, and the assistant's answers feed records or decisions, the output criterion (PI1.4 in the 2017 Trust Services Criteria) is about delivering output completely and accurately; a recorded quote check and a question set run before each release are the kind of evidence an auditor asks for, so build them in now rather than before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's HR assistant answers staff questions from the policy handbook. An employee asks about parental leave and gets: Parents may take 26 weeks of paid leave (section 4.2). Section 4.2 exists, but it says: Parents may take up to 26 weeks of leave, of which 12 are paid. Nobody has edited the handbook. What probably happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The model wrote the quotation itself, from memory of the chunk, and changed the words; it wasn't copied from the source
Use citations, so the quoted text is copied from the handbook with its location
Check every quotation by string match against the text it cites, and strike or flag what fails

recall.model: The model probably wrote that quotation from memory of the chunk instead of copying it, and in rewriting it lost "up to" and "of which 12 are paid", so the words read as a quotation but aren't in section 4.2. I'd turn on citations, so the quoted text is copied from the handbook with its section rather than written by the model, keeping each section as its own block with its number. Then I'd add a quote check: string match every quotation in the answer against the text it cites, and strike any that isn't there before the answer is sent. I'd also allow "not found" and measure faithfulness on a fixed set of HR questions.

recall.prompt: You send a deposition transcript to Anthropic's citations feature and want every cited span to belong to exactly one named speaker. Which way of sending it does that?
options: As plain text, cut into sentences automatically and cited by character index
As a PDF, cut into sentences and cited by page number
As a custom content document with one block per speaker turn, the name at the start
As plain text with temperature 0, so the citations are always the same
recall.why: Custom content documents use your blocks as they are, and a citation names a range of whole blocks, with cited text copied from them. With one block per speaker turn and the name in each block, a cited span is whole turns with their names on, never a fragment from inside two speakers. Sentence chunking can't see speakers, and temperature has nothing to do with citations.

recall.prompt: Your team's RAG assistant looks good in demos. Before it goes to customers, your manager asks for a number showing how often it makes things up. How would you produce it?

keyIdeas.idea: Build a fixed set of questions with known answers, including some the documents can't answer
Split each answer into claims and report supported claims divided by all claims: faithfulness
Also count honest not found answers and answerable questions left unanswered, so refusing everything can't score well

recall.model: I'd build a fixed set of questions with known answers from our documents, including some the documents can't answer. For each answer, split it into claims and check each claim against the source, by string match for quotations and by a person or a second model for the rest, then report supported claims divided by all claims, which is faithfulness. Beside it I'd report how many unanswerable questions got an honest not found and how many answerable ones were left unanswered, because an assistant that refuses everything makes no claims and would look perfect. Then I'd rerun the set before every change.

recall.prompt: A colleague says setting temperature to 0 will stop the assistant inventing quotations. What does temperature 0 actually give you?
options: Faithful answers, because only the likeliest words are chosen
More repeatable answers, wrong ones included, and not fully deterministic
Citations that always point at the right block
Fewer input tokens on every request
recall.why: Temperature changes how the next word is drawn, not what the model was given. A stitched quote from a nameless chunk can be the likeliest text, so at 0 it comes back every time. Anthropic's API reference says even temperature 0 isn't fully deterministic, and its newer models accept only 1.0.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The blocks, citations and quote check have held: not one invented line since that Monday. The agency now runs my eight questions and 52 more every week, and the dashboard shows faithfulness at 100% every week. In September someone tightened the system prompt to: if in any doubt, say not found. Now the lawyers ring me at night. Last week 61 of 160 answers were not found, up from 14 a night in August, and I read ten of them against the transcripts: in seven the answer was on the page. The dashboard still says 100%.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does faithfulness still read 100%, and what should the agency measure as well?

keyIdeas.idea: Faithfulness counts only the claims that are sent; a not found makes no claim, so refusing more can't lower it
Measure how many answerable questions get an answer, on a set that marks which questions the transcripts answer
Track both numbers together and roll back or reject a change that raises not found on answerable questions

coldCase.model: Faithfulness divides supported claims by claims sent. A not found makes no claim, so it isn't counted at all: the new prompt removed claims, and the share of what's left that is supported stayed at 100%. An assistant that answered nothing would score the same. The agency needs a second number from the same set: of the questions the transcripts do answer, how many got an answer, the answerable questions left unanswered. Mark each question in the set as answerable or not, report both numbers together on the dashboard, and roll back the September prompt change, which raised not found on answerable questions; from now on, reject any change that improves one number by wrecking the other.

sources.title: Anthropic, Citations (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: ground Claude's responses in your source documents; compared to prompting Claude to cite sources, cited_text does not count toward your output tokens, and because the API parses citations and extracts cited_text directly, citations are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents; document types plain text (sentence chunking, character indices, 0-indexed), PDF (sentence chunking, page numbers, 1-indexed) and custom content (lists, transcripts, special formatting, more granular citations; no additional chunking; block indices, 0-indexed); if you need more control over citation granularity (for example, for bullet points or transcripts), use custom content documents instead; citations and structured outputs are incompatible and return a 400 error

Anthropic, Create a Message (Claude API reference), read 11 October 2026: CitationContentBlockLocation, cited_text is the full text of the cited block range, always equals the contents of content[start_block_index:end_block_index] joined together, the text block is the minimal citable unit and this field is never a substring of a single block; end_block_index exclusive; temperature deprecated, models released after Claude Opus 4.6 do not support setting temperature, a value of 1.0 is accepted for backwards compatibility and all other values are rejected with a 400 error; even with temperature of 0.0 the results will not be fully deterministic

Anthropic, Reduce hallucinations (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: allow Claude to say I don't know, explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty; use direct quotes for factual grounding; verify with citations, have Claude verify each claim by finding a supporting quote after it generates a response, and if it can't find a quote, it must retract the claim

Cohere, RAG Citations (API v2 documentation), read 11 October 2026: the Chat endpoint generates fine-grained citations for its RAG response; each citation has the start and end indices of the text that cites a source, its corresponding span of text, and the source or sources it references

Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke and Steven Schockaert, Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation, 2023 (arXiv 2309.15217): the answer is faithful to the context if the claims that are made in the answer can be inferred from the context; final faithfulness score F = |V|/|S|, where |V| is the number of statements that were supported and |S| the total number of statements
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including the processing integrity category and its output criterion, PI1.4
